location.evidence: The top programs lean toward Massachusetts and the bottom ones toward New York, but these are highly selective and less selective schools. That points to selectivity, not to the regional pay for economics jobs.

prestige.evidence: The best-paying economics programs are at schools that admit very few applicants. Duke's economics department reports that most of its graduates who take jobs go into finance, and many of the rest go into consulting.

stepping_stone.evidence: Many economics majors go on to graduate school, most often law school or an MBA. These degrees usually come after a few years of work, so first-year earnings capture only part of the picture.

programs.evidence: Claremont McKenna is highly selective. Its economics career office holds employer information sessions and industry nights focused on careers in finance, consulting and accounting.
Duke is highly selective, and its economics department reports that most graduates who take jobs go into finance or management consulting.
Harvard admits almost no one, and student surveys show a large share of its working graduates go into high-paying finance and consulting jobs.
Nothing found about Purchase's economics program, such as admissions, format or graduate destinations, explains why its graduates earn less.
Federal wage data show that pay in the Albuquerque area falls below the national average, which helps explain lower starting pay for local graduates.
The earnings figure comes from too few graduates to be reliable.
